title: Healthcare
subtitle: GP, locum, primary care, prescription charge
summary: Name the people and parts of a healthcare system - GPs, locums and specialists, primary and secondary care, prescriptions and insurance schemes.

lesson.heading: Primary care
lesson.text: **Primary care** is provided by the doctors (also called **physicians**) or nurses a patient goes to first. This may happen at the doctor's **surgery** or during a **home visit**. A **locum** is a doctor who does the job of another doctor who is ill or on holiday. Most care is provided through the primary care system, whether the problem is an **acute condition** - one that is severe and sudden in onset - or a **chronic** one, which keeps coming back.

examples.text: I need to phone the **surgery** to make an appointment for a blood test.
I saw a very nice **locum** today because our normal GP was on leave.
He suffers from **chronic** bronchitis - it comes back year after year.
Lydia had her appendix removed after an **acute** attack of appendicitis.

lesson.note: Do doctors often do home visits in your country? Not ~~home visitors~~.

lesson.heading: Secondary care and referral
lesson.text: **Secondary care** is provided by **specialists** in special clinics or hospitals. Patients are **referred to** a specialist by their own doctor. Specialists may concentrate on one **organ** - a part of the body such as the stomach or liver - or on a specific age group.

examples.text: The GP decided to **refer** Alex to a specialist.
The heart is the **organ** which pumps blood around our bodies.
Chris has a skin **condition** which is taking a long time to clear up.

lesson.heading: Specialists and what they specialise in
rows: anaesthesia - stopping people feeling pain during surgery

lesson.heading: Alternative or complementary medicine
rows: treats patients using needles at special points around the skin
treats patients by pressing joints, for example in the spine or backbone
uses tiny amounts of natural substances to treat an illness
lesson.note: These approaches differ from conventional western medicine. The correct adjectives are alternative medicine and complementary medicine - not ~~alternating~~ or ~~complimentary~~.

lesson.heading: Paying for healthcare in Britain
lesson.text: **Healthcare** is the general expression for all the services offered by hospitals, clinics, dentists and opticians. In Britain it is paid for through taxes and **national insurance** payments taken directly from wages. The government decides how much will be spent on the **National Health Service** (the **NHS**), though many people feel it does not spend enough.

examples.text: **National insurance** is paid by most working adults and covers the cost of healthcare for everyone.
Hospital treatment and visits to a **family doctor** are free.

lesson.heading: GPs, prescriptions and going private
lesson.text: A **GP** - general practitioner - is a doctor who looks after people's general health. A **surgery** is a small centre offering primary care run by one GP or a group of them; a **clinic** specialises in a particular condition. Treatment is free, but there is often a **prescription charge**, which you pay at a pharmacy. Private healthcare is available and many **insurance schemes** exist to enable people to **go private**.

examples.text: The doctor wrote me a **prescription** for some painkillers.
Is there a **prescription charge** in your country?
Are there **insurance schemes** for private healthcare in your country?
When it comes to healthcare, do many people in your country **go private**?

lesson.text: Acute and chronic are opposites of a kind: acute means severe and sudden, chronic means long-lasting and recurring.

exercises.prompt: Match each specialist with what they specialise in.
